content.text:
**Short answer:** I wouldn’t call gold clearly undervalued today. I’d call it **fair-to-expensive on traditional valuation measures**, but **still potentially attractive as insurance** if you think geopolitical risk, fiscal stress, dollar distrust, or central-bank buying will remain elevated.

As of **June 8, 2026**, spot gold was around **$4,320–$4,330/oz**, after hitting a two-month low amid stronger U.S. jobs data and renewed expectations of higher rates. ([marketscreener.com](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/gold-erases-losses-after-ceasefire-hopes-emerge-strong-us-jobs-data-caps-gains-ce7f5dd3d981f125?utm_source=openai))

### Why gold *could* still be undervalued
- **Central banks are still buying aggressively.** The World Gold Council reported estimated net central-bank purchases of **244 tonnes in Q1 2026**, continuing the post-2022 trend of large official-sector demand. ([gold.org](https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-demand-trends/gold-demand-trends-q1-2026/central-banks?utm_source=openai))  
- **Structural demand has changed.** Gold is increasingly being treated not just as an inflation hedge, but as a hedge against sanctions risk, fiscal risk, currency debasement, and geopolitical fragmentation.
- **Many bank targets are still above spot.** Reuters-reported forecasts include JPMorgan at **$6,300/oz by end-2026** and UBS having raised targets to **$6,200/oz** earlier this year. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/jp-morgan-sees-yearend-2026-gold-price-at-6300-per-ounce-4523320?utm_source=openai)) If those are right, today’s price would look undervalued.

### Why gold may *not* be undervalued
- **It’s already had a huge run.** Gold reached record levels above **$5,400/oz** earlier in 2026 before pulling back. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/3f41d4a3e41dd721875687d2f4aeaeb7?utm_source=openai))  
- **Higher real rates are a headwind.** Gold pays no yield, so rising Treasury yields and a stronger dollar make it less attractive; recent weakness has been tied to rate-hike fears. ([kitco.com](https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-19/gold-falls-more-1-treasury-yields-dollar-weigh-amid-inflation-concerns?utm_source=openai))  
- **Jewelry demand is price-sensitive.** The World Gold Council notes that high prices and volatility are shifting demand dynamics, with investment and central-bank demand offsetting weaker consumer demand. ([gold.org](https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-demand-trends/gold-demand-trends-q1-2026?utm_source=openai))

### My take
If you mean **“undervalued versus history”**, probably **no**—gold is expensive relative to most past price regimes.

If you mean **“undervalued versus the current macro environment”**, maybe **moderately**—but only if you believe the world is moving into a lasting regime of:
- persistent inflation risk,
- weaker confidence in fiat currencies,
- large fiscal deficits,
- geopolitical fragmentation,
- and continued central-bank diversification away from dollar assets.

For a portfolio, I’d view gold less as a screaming bargain and more as **crisis insurance**. A **5–10% allocation** can make sense for diversification, but going heavily overweight after such a large rally is risky unless you have a strong macro thesis.
